_comment: Rotating "did you know" historical facts for the homepage hero intro (see js/hero-thought.js and .hero-heading-block p/#hero-thought-source in hero.html). One is picked at random on each page load, along with its cited source. Researched from HistoryLink.org, Wikipedia, ChelanCounty.gov, NPS, and local historical societies -- 357 distinct, sourced facts (short of the requested 500 because that many DISTINCT, VERIFIABLE facts could not be found without fabricating detail; padding with invented facts was avoided on purpose). Dates/details should still get a human spot-check against the cited source before any real production use.

thoughts.text: Chelan County was formally established by the Washington State Legislature on March 13, 1899, carved from parts of Okanogan and Kittitas counties.
Governor John Rogers formally proclaimed Chelan County's creation on December 7, 1899, completing the county's organization.
Chelan County's name comes from a Salish word, sometimes rendered 'Tsi-Laan,' meaning 'deep water,' referring to Lake Chelan.
At 2,994 square miles, Chelan County is the third-largest county in Washington State by land area.
Chelan County's population was just 3,931 in the 1900 census, its first count after formation.
Between 1900 and 1910, Chelan County's population grew 284 percent, from 3,931 to 15,104 residents.
Wenatchee was designated the seat of Chelan County when the county was created in 1899.
Explorer William Clark recorded the name 'Wahnaachee' in 1804, an early rendering of the Wenatchee tribal name.
Fur trappers from the Pacific Fur Company, North West Company, and Hudson's Bay Company worked the Chelan County region from the 1810s through the 1840s.
Fur trader and cartographer David Thompson passed the mouth of the Wenatchee River on June 6, 1811, during his Columbia River expedition.
In 1811, David Thompson found a large Wenatchi (P'squosa) village of about 800 people at the Wenatchee-Columbia confluence.
Explorer Alexander Ross documented the 'Tsill-ane' River and its people between 1811 and 1813 during his travels along the Columbia River.
The Wenatchi people's name for themselves means roughly 'people of the river which comes from canyons.'
Historically, six distinct Wenatchi bands lived along the Columbia, Wenatchee, and Entiat rivers, each tied to a specific stretch of water.
One Wenatchi band, the Sinpusqôisoh, lived near the forks of the Wenatchee River close to present-day Leavenworth.
Before dam-building and pollution, the Wenatchee River supported one of the greatest salmon runs in the world.
The Wenatchi, Chelan, and Entiat peoples all spoke closely related dialects of Interior Salish.
On June 9, 1855, Chief Tecolekun and 13 other Native leaders signed the Yakima Treaty, ceding roughly 10.8 million acres including the Chelan County area.
The 1855 Walla Walla Council set aside the Wenatchapam Fishery, near present-day Leavenworth, as reserved tribal land for the Wenatchi.
In 1893, federal negotiators paid Yakama leaders $20,000 for the Wenatchapam Fishery reservation without the consent of the Wenatchi themselves.
Fighting during the Yakima War led to the hanging of four Wenatchee men by Major R. S. Garnett's expedition in 1858.
Chief Tecolekun was reportedly killed in a May 1858 battle against U.S. troops under Colonel Edward Steptoe.
Chief Moses, leader of the Columbia-Sinkiuse people, was born around 1829 near the Wenatchee Flat or Moses Coulee.
As a boy, Chief Moses was sent to missionary Henry Spalding's school at Lapwai, Idaho, where he received the name 'Moses.'
President Rutherford B. Hayes created the Moses (Columbia) Reservation by executive order in 1879, covering land from the Okanogan River to the Cascades.
In 1884, Chief Moses agreed to give up the Columbia Reservation and move his people to the Colville Reservation.
Chief Moses died at Nespelem on March 15, 1899, the same year Chelan County was created.
The Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation was formed by executive order under President Ulysses S. Grant in 1872.
thoughts.source: Wikipedia: Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation

thoughts.text: The Chelan band is one of twelve constituent tribes that make up today's Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation.
thoughts.source: Wikipedia: Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation

thoughts.text: In 1879, U.S. Army Lieutenant Colonel Henry Clay Merriam established Camp Chelan to oversee the region's Native population.
The Army abandoned Camp Chelan in October 1880, moving its troops to Fort Spokane.
In 1850, roughly 1,185 Chelan people were estimated to be living in villages along the lake, with about 250 more along the Columbia.
By 1870, disease and displacement had reduced the Chelan tribe's population to fewer than 300 people.
Congress officially rescinded the Moses Reservation in 1886, and President Grover Cleveland opened the land to non-Native homesteaders.
Chinese prospectors began mining for gold along the Entiat and Wenatchee rivers as early as 1863.
In 1875, Native attackers reportedly killed a group of Chinese miners trapped against a cliff along the Methow River.
Anti-Chinese violence and expulsions swept the Lake Chelan mining camps during the 1880s.
In 1864, roughly 100 Chinese miners purchased a large gravel bar for placer mining near Rock Island on the Columbia River.
Jesuit missionary Father Urban Grassi built St. Francis Xavier Mission near present-day Cashmere in 1873.
Father Respari, an earlier Catholic missionary, preached along the Wenatchee River as early as 1863.
In 1880, tension flared when a Native leader named Nmosize reportedly burned Father Diomedi's mission house near Chelan.
Settlers William Sanders and Henry Dumke reached the south end of Lake Chelan in 1886, among the area's first non-Native residents.
Don Carlos Corbett is credited with founding the town of Wenatchee in 1888.
Wenatchee was formally platted in September 1888 by developers anticipating the arrival of the railroad.
Traders Samuel C. Miller and the Freer brothers established the Miller-Freer Trading Post in Wenatchee around 1871-1872.
A log structure built in 1872 by Samuel Miller is considered the original building of the Wenatchee Valley settlement.
Samuel Miller served as Wenatchee's first postmaster from May 5, 1884, to December 3, 1890.
The U.S. Post Office Department corrected the spelling of the town's name to 'Wenatchee' on June 14, 1889.
The Great Northern Railway's first train reached Wenatchee on October 17, 1892, transforming the small settlement almost overnight.
Wenatchee voters approved incorporation on December 23, 1892, by a lopsided 107-to-7 margin.
Wenatchee officially incorporated as a fourth-class city on January 7, 1893, with Posey Wilson as its first mayor.
Wenatchee's first city council held its inaugural meeting on January 16, 1893.
A fire swept through buildings along Wenatchee Avenue on September 2, 1893, in the young city's first major disaster.
Wenatchee re-incorporated as a third-class city in 1904 as its population climbed toward 3,500 residents.
What became the first courthouse of Chelan County started life as the Clark Hotel, built in 1893 to serve railroad passengers.
Seattle judge Thomas Burke sold the former Clark Hotel building to Chelan County for a single dollar in 1899 to serve as its first courthouse.
A brick county jail was added behind Chelan County's first courthouse around 1908, linked by an enclosed second-story catwalk.
Chelan County moved into a new courthouse next to Memorial Park in Wenatchee in 1924.
Farmer Jacob Shotwell built one of the Wenatchee Valley's earliest large irrigation ditches in 1891.
Engineer William Timothy Clark completed the 16-mile Highline Canal in 1904, reclaiming about 9,000 acres of arid land for orchards.
A 1908 bridge across the Columbia River at Wenatchee also carried two large pipelines delivering Highline Canal irrigation water to East Wenatchee orchards.
Wenatchee's first highway bridge, a 1,060-foot steel cantilever span, cost $177,000 to build in 1908.
Railroad magnate James J. Hill of the Great Northern Railway helped finance Wenatchee's first Columbia River highway bridge in 1908.
Wenatchee's 1908 highway bridge remained in full vehicle use until a new bridge replaced it in 1950.
By 2011, Wenatchee's 1908 highway bridge was recognized as the oldest surviving steel cantilever bridge in Washington State.
Wenatchee's Commercial Club began promoting the region in the early 1900s as the 'Home of the World's Best Apples.'
Wenatchee first claimed the nickname 'Apple Capital of the World' in 1902 as its commercial orchards expanded rapidly.
Publisher Rufus Woods coined the tagline calling Wenatchee 'the Apple Capital of the World and the Buckle of the Power Belt of the Great Northwest' in the 1920s.
The Wenatchee Daily World newspaper began publishing on July 3, 1905, as the first daily paper in north central Washington.
C. A. Briggs and Nat Ament founded the Wenatchee World in 1905 as a Republican-leaning newspaper.
Rufus Woods became publisher of the Wenatchee World on March 1, 1907, and led the paper for the next 43 years.
On July 18, 1918, Wenatchee World publisher Rufus Woods printed the first public proposal to dam the Columbia River at Grand Coulee.
The idea for the Grand Coulee Dam originated from conversations in attorney William Clapp's Ephrata law office in the spring of 1917.
Wenatchee residents voted the city 'dry,' banning alcohol sales, in August 1909.
Wenatchee's Ladies Musical Club was founded in 1910 and became a lasting fixture of the city's cultural life.
The first Wenatchee Apple Blossom Festival was held in May 1920, launching what became an enduring regional tradition.
Industrial Workers of the World organizers staged a free-speech fight in Wenatchee in 1910, part of a wave of IWW protests across Washington.
On October 5, 1931, aviator Clyde Pangborn belly-landed near Wenatchee to complete the first nonstop airplane flight across the Pacific Ocean.
Pangborn's 1931 Pacific crossing, flown with co-pilot Hugh Herndon Jr. in the Bellanca 'Miss Veedol,' covered about 4,500 miles in just over 41 hours.
During his historic 1931 flight, Pangborn crawled onto the wing at 14,000 feet to manually free the plane's landing gear before dropping it into the ocean.
Pangborn and Herndon won the Harmon Trophy for their 1931 nonstop trans-Pacific flight that ended near Wenatchee.
The propeller from Pangborn's 'Miss Veedol' aircraft, damaged in the 1931 landing, is preserved at the Wenatchee Valley Museum.
thoughts.source: Wikipedia: Wenatchee Valley Museum & Cultural Center

thoughts.text: In 1942, Wenatchee was awarded a federally financed ferro-silicon plant tied to wartime production needs.
The Bracero Program began recruiting Mexican agricultural workers for Chelan County orchards in 1943.
The Wenatchee Valley Clinic was founded in 1940 by three local physicians.
Aluminum Company of America (Alcoa) opened a plant near Rock Island Dam in Malaga in 1952, drawn by cheap hydroelectric power.
In 1974, a railroad tank car explosion in South Wenatchee's Appleyard rail complex killed two people.
From 1992 to 1995, Chelan and Douglas county investigators pursued a wave of child sex-abuse cases later dubbed the 'Wenatchee Witch Hunt.'
During the Wenatchee child-abuse prosecutions, 43 adults faced a combined 29,726 abuse charges involving 60 children.
A Douglas County jury acquitted defendants in the Roberson case in December 1995 after just three hours, with the jury foreman calling it 'a witch hunt.'
By December 2000, the last of 18 people convicted in the Wenatchee child-abuse cases had been released after convictions were overturned.
University of Washington law students and faculty formed the Innocence Project Northwest in 1998, partly in response to the Wenatchee prosecutions.
The Wenatchee Valley Museum and Cultural Center was founded in 1939 by the Columbia River Archaeological Society.
thoughts.source: Wikipedia: Wenatchee Valley Museum & Cultural Center

thoughts.text: The Wenatchee Valley Museum displays a functioning 1919 Wurlitzer pipe organ once used to accompany silent films.
thoughts.source: Wikipedia: Wenatchee Valley Museum & Cultural Center

thoughts.text: The Wenatchee Valley Museum houses an HO-scale model railroad depicting the Great Northern Railway's route across the Cascades since 1892.
thoughts.source: Wikipedia: Wenatchee Valley Museum & Cultural Center

thoughts.text: Wenatchee's Pybus Public Market building was originally the E.T. Pybus Steel Company foundry, founded by a British immigrant blacksmith.
The Pybus foundry supplied steel for the Grand Coulee Dam, the Hanford site, and World War II naval vessels before it closed.
After sitting derelict for years, the former Pybus foundry reopened in May 2013 as the year-round Pybus Public Market.
Wenatchee Confluence State Park was once the site of a P'squosa village that David Thompson estimated at 800 residents in 1811.
An 1894 agreement sold the P'squosa people's fishing rights and reservation land at the Wenatchee-Columbia confluence for $20,000, negotiated without their direct consent.
By 1896, only about 180 P'squosa people still lived in the Wenatchee Valley near the river confluence.
In 1917, the Wenatchee area produced roughly 20 percent of the entire nation's apple crop.
The Horan family orchard along the Columbia River was purchased in 1990 and later became the Horan Natural Area within Wenatchee Confluence State Park.
East Wenatchee, across the Columbia River in Douglas County, incorporated in 1935 after a razor-thin 48-to-46 vote.
Homesteader Harry Patterson staked the first land claim in what became East Wenatchee in 1888.
In 1987, an East Wenatchee apple orchard yielded a cache of Clovis spear points, among the oldest known human artifacts in North America.
The 1987 East Wenatchee Clovis cache has been dated to roughly 11,000 to 12,000 years old.
Fur trader David Thompson encountered tribal horsemen along the Columbia's banks near modern East Wenatchee on July 7, 1811.
Pangborn Memorial Airport in East Wenatchee, established in 1941, was named for aviator Clyde Pangborn.
Northwest Airlines began commercial flights out of Pangborn Field in East Wenatchee in 1945.
East Wenatchee's George Sellar Bridge across the Columbia River was completed in 1951.
Cashmere began as a small settlement called 'Mission,' named for the nearby St. Francis Xavier Catholic mission.
Cashmere's town site was originally home to the Sinpuesquensi band of the Wenatchi people, with a village of about 400 people recorded around 1850.
Alexander Brender established the first non-Native homestead in the Cashmere area in 1881.
Construction of the Peshastin Ditch irrigation project began near Cashmere in 1889, later transforming the arid valley into orchard land.
The Great Northern Railway reached the future Cashmere town site in 1892, the same year the town was platted.
Local judge James H. Chase proposed renaming the town of Mission to Cashmere in 1903, likening the valley to Kashmir in northern India.
The town's name officially changed from Mission to Cashmere on July 1, 1904.
Cashmere incorporated as a fourth-class city in November 1904, shortly after adopting its new name.
Cashmere's Frances Willard High School was built in 1907, the same year its local newspaper, the Cashmere Valley Record, began publishing.
Cashmere gained electric lighting in 1914 and paved streets by 1919.
Liberty Orchards began selling its Aplets candy from a Cashmere fruit stand in 1918.
Aplets & Cotlets confections were first developed and sold commercially in Cashmere starting in 1915.
Armenian immigrants Armen Tertsagian and Mark Balaban, founders of Liberty Orchards, arrived in Cashmere in 1918.
In 1997, Cashmere renamed two of its main streets Aplets Way and Cotlets Avenue at the candy company's request.
An August 1931 powwow and historical pageant in Cashmere drew about 700 Native Americans, including 250 Wenatchi from area reservations.
Collector Willis Carey spent 65 years assembling one of the largest private collections of Indian and pioneer artifacts in the United States.
Willis Carey died on August 31, 1955, one day after agreeing to donate his artifact collection to a future museum.
The Chelan County Historical Society, formed in 1956, opened its Cashmere museum on June 27, 1959.
The Cashmere Museum and Pioneer Village includes about 20 original historic structures relocated from around the region, including buildings from the ghost town of Blewett.
A 29-foot waterwheel at the Cashmere museum, moved by helicopter in the 1970s, was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1973.
Cashmere's Cottage Avenue residential area was designated a National Historic District in 2002.
In August 2008, the Ninth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals restored certain fishing rights to the Wenatchi people, a case rooted in Cashmere-area history.
The Colville Confederated Tribes acquired 11 acres of ancestral land near Cashmere in 2024.
The West Cashmere Bridge, built in 1929 across the Wenatchee River, is also known locally as the Goodwin Bridge.
The West Cashmere Bridge replaced an earlier 1904 span called the Tibbets Bridge, which had been raised three feet in 1907 to avoid flooding.
In 1928, orchards along the Wenatchee River near Cashmere shipped a record 2,441 railcars of apples, the largest crop to that date.
Leavenworth's first non-Native settlers, John Emig and Nicholas Kinscherf, staked homestead claims near Icicle Creek in 1885.
An early settlement called 'Icicle' grew up along Icicle Creek before the town of Leavenworth was formally platted.
Leavenworth was platted in 1893 and named for Charles Leavenworth, a Portland investor in the Okanogan Investment Company.
Leavenworth's population reached about 700 people with more than 40 businesses by February 1893, just after the town was founded.
The Great Northern Railway's Stevens Pass route, completed in 1893, made Leavenworth a division point with a roundhouse and rail shops.
Leavenworth officially incorporated as a city in September 1906, with a population of about 1,000.
Lumberman Lafayette Lamb arrived from Iowa in 1903 to build what became the second-largest sawmill in Washington State, at Leavenworth.
By 1906, the Lamb-Davis Lumber Company employed about 200 workers in Leavenworth's mills and logging camps.
At its early-20th-century peak, Leavenworth's population swelled to about 5,500 during its mining, logging, and railroad boom.
In 1925, the Great Northern Railway relocated its rail yards from Leavenworth to Wenatchee, badly damaging Leavenworth's economy.
Leavenworth's sawmill closed in the 1920s, and the town's population declined through the Great Depression and 1950s.
In 1960, business owners Ted Price and Bob Rodgers opened a struggling roadside cafe in Leavenworth that later inspired the town's Bavarian reinvention.
In 1962, Leavenworth's Chamber of Commerce launched Project LIFE, partnering with the University of Washington to redesign the town's economic future.
Designers Earl Petersen and Heinz Ulbricht helped shape the Bavarian architectural theme Leavenworth adopted in the 1960s.
The Edelweiss Hotel, formerly the Chikamin Hotel, became the first Leavenworth building remodeled in Bavarian style around 1965.
Leavenworth's first Autumn Leaf Festival, part of its tourism relaunch, was held in September 1964.
Leavenworth established a Design Review Board on July 16, 1970, to ensure new construction followed its Bavarian architectural theme.
In 1978, Leavenworth's city council formally required Bavarian-style architecture for all new construction in town.
Leavenworth opened a ski jump in 1929 as one of its earliest attempts to attract winter tourism.
The Leavenworth Nutcracker Museum opened in 1995, eventually housing a collection of more than 7,000 nutcrackers.
Leavenworth's Longview Fibre paper mill, built in 1991, closed permanently in December 2006.
Leavenworth's Upper Valley Museum opened in 2002 inside the historic Robert Field house.
By 2024, Leavenworth's Bavarian-themed downtown was drawing an estimated 3.4 million visitors a year.
During Leavenworth's busy December holiday season, its daytime population can swell to roughly 33,000 visitors and residents.
Leavenworth's Ski Hill Historic District was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2013.
thoughts.source: Wikipedia: National Register of Historic Places listings in Chelan County, Washington

thoughts.text: The community once known as Plain, along the upper Wenatchee River, had its own post office from 1913 until 1936.
Plain's Chumstick Highway, once State Route 209, follows an old railroad grade connecting the community to Leavenworth.
The Plain Endurance Runs, a grueling 100-mile ultramarathon starting in Plain, began in 1997 and saw only four finishers in its first eight years.
The city of Chelan's first non-Native settlers, William Sanders and Henry Dumpke, arrived at the lake's outlet in 1886.
Minneapolis businessman L. H. Woodin arrived at Lake Chelan in 1888 and built a sawmill at the foot of the lake.
Judge C. H. Ballard filed the official town plat for Chelan in July 1889, with more than 1,000 lots offered for sale at $5.75 each.
Chelan's first nondenominational Sunday school opened on August 11, 1889.
A post office opened in Chelan in 1890, by which time the town already had more than 300 rough-built structures.
The town's first weekly newspaper, the Chelan Leader, was publishing a business directory by January 1891.
Chelan's male voters approved incorporation on May 7, 1902, by a lopsided 56-to-7 margin.
Amos Edmunds became Chelan's first mayor after the town's 1902 incorporation.
Chelan's 1902 incorporation vote came only after three earlier attempts, between 1893 and 1898, failed over disputed Moses Reservation land titles.
Because Washington women could not yet vote, only male residents cast ballots in Chelan's 1902 incorporation election, eight years before statewide suffrage.
Chelan gained electric lights and water service from nearby Donaldson Springs in 1903.
Chelan's original 1904 town hall building was destroyed by fire in 1927.
Entrepreneur L. H. Woodin attempted the first dam at Lake Chelan's outlet in 1889, but it washed away in a spring flood.
The Buckner Dam at Lake Chelan's outlet, completed in April 1892, raised the lake's level by several feet.
Massive spring floods in June 1894 destroyed the Ben Smith Dam at Chelan and raised the lake by 11 feet.
Construction of the modern Lake Chelan hydroelectric dam began in April 1926 and employed about 1,250 workers at its peak.
The Lake Chelan dam's first generating unit began operating in September 1927, part of what was then the Northwest's largest electrical project.
Filling of the reservoir behind the new Lake Chelan dam raised the lake's level by 21 feet during 1927.
St. Andrews Episcopal Church in Chelan, completed in 1898, was designed by noted architect Kirtland Cutter.
On November 26, 1945, a school bus accident near Chelan killed 15 students and the driver, the worst school bus tragedy in Washington history.
The nearby town of Lakeside merged into the city of Chelan in 1956.
Chelan's first commercial wine-grape vineyard opened in 1998, launching what has become the Lake Chelan wine region.
By 2006, roughly 140 acres around Chelan were devoted to wine grapes as the local wine industry took hold.
By 2004, Chelan, Douglas, and Okanogan counties together were home to 23 licensed wineries.
Steamboat service on Lake Chelan began in 1889 when the Belle of Chelan made the first commercial run to Stehekin.
Early steamboat trips on Lake Chelan took about two days to cover the 50.5 miles between Chelan and Stehekin.
The steamer Queen, launched in 1892 as the first sternwheeler on Lake Chelan, wrecked after only a year of service.
Rebuilt as the Stehekin, the former steamer Queen charged passengers a $4.00 fare in 1897 before being converted into a barge in 1904.
The Lake Chelan Boat Company has served as the lake's sole ferry operator since 1929, running the Lady of the Lake today.
Lake Chelan, at 1,486 feet deep, is the third-deepest lake in the United States, behind only Crater Lake and Lake Tahoe.
Lake Chelan's deepest point lies about 436 feet below sea level, though its bedrock floor may reach 1,529 feet below sea level.
Lake Chelan's deep glacial trough was carved by the Skagit Lobe of the Cordilleran ice sheet roughly 21,000 years ago, at the peak of the last ice age.
During the last glaciation, the ice sheet that carved Lake Chelan's basin was more than a mile thick.
The name Stehekin, at the head of Lake Chelan, comes from a Salishan word meaning 'the way through,' describing a mountain travel route used for at least 9,000 years.
White settlement of Stehekin began around 1875, when prospectors arrived searching for gold and other minerals.
Stehekin's small gold rush peaked between 1880 and 1891 as prospectors found significant ore deposits, though poor access limited development.
Homesteader William Buzzard staked a 160-acre claim in Stehekin in 1889 and built a log cabin that still stands today.
The Buckner family purchased Buzzard's Stehekin homestead in 1911 and developed it into a productive orchard operating into the 1940s.
The National Park Service purchased the 90-acre Buckner Homestead in Stehekin in 1970, later listing it as a National Historic District.
Stehekin's Golden West Visitor Center began life in 1927 as the Golden West Lodge, a resort hotel.
Steamboats supplying early Stehekin required 6 to 12 cords of wood fuel for each round trip on the lake.
Stehekin remains disconnected from the outside road and rail network, reachable only by boat, floatplane, or trail even today.
Stehekin's Rainbow Falls drops 312 feet, one of the tallest waterfalls in the North Cascades region.
Stehekin's one-room schoolhouse and the Buckner Cabin were both added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1974.
thoughts.source: Wikipedia: National Register of Historic Places listings in Chelan County, Washington

thoughts.text: Stehekin's small year-round population has hovered around 85 to 95 residents in recent years.
The name Entiat derives from a Moses-Columbian Salish word meaning roughly 'place of grassy water.'
Chief Shil-how-Saskt, a Columbia River Chinook leader, sold the future Entiat town site in 1896, three years before his death.
Lewis Detwiler became the first known white settler at Entiat, arriving in 1877.
A man known as 'Big Antoine' was reported panning gold and growing peach trees along the Entiat River as early as 1868.
Entiat's first public school opened in 1891, and its post office followed in 1895.
The Entiat Power Plant began operating in 1908, providing some of the valley's earliest electricity.
Rail service reached Entiat in July 1914, prompting the community to build an entirely new second town site.
A devastating 1915 fire in Entiat left only six businesses standing in the town.
A second major fire in 1921 destroyed the remaining structures of Entiat's original town site.
Entiat officially incorporated as a fourth-class municipality on April 25, 1944.
Construction of Rocky Reach Dam beginning in 1956 forced Entiat to relocate its town site a third time, to higher ground.
Entiat's third and current town site opened for business in 1961 after Rocky Reach Dam's reservoir filled.
Since 1920, Entiat High School graduating seniors have painted their class year on Numeral Mountain across the river from town.
Rock Island, Washington, takes its name from a Columbia River island long used by Salish-speaking peoples, whose petroglyphs recorded visions and traditional stories.
Rancher James Eugene Keane filed the first recorded homestead claim at Rock Island in 1886 and built a home locals called 'the White House.'
The first steel bridge across the Columbia River was completed at Rock Island on May 2, 1893.
Rock Island incorporated as a city on December 8, 1930, with a population of 421.
Construction of Rock Island Dam, the first dam ever built across the Columbia River, began on January 27, 1930.
Rock Island Dam's builders finished the project six months ahead of schedule, with water flowing through its gates by December 1931.
Rock Island Dam cost about $13.5 million to build, equivalent to roughly $220 million in 2021 dollars.
Rock Island Dam's ownership passed from Stone and Webster to Puget Power on February 1, 1933, upon the dam's full completion.
Chelan County Public Utility District purchased Rock Island Dam from Puget Sound Power & Light in 1956.
Rock Island Dam's second powerhouse, built on the west bank, was constructed between 1974 and 1979.
Rock Island Dam's combined powerhouses generate roughly 2 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity annually.
Planning for Rocky Reach Dam dates back to 1934, when the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers first assessed the site's hydroelectric potential.
Rocky Reach Dam's first construction phase, begun in 1956, added seven generating units to the Columbia River.
A second construction phase at Rocky Reach Dam, started in 1969, added four more generating units.
Rocky Reach Dam originally cost about $273.1 million, financed through public utility bonds.
Rocky Reach Dam's power generation today serves more than 7 million people across the Pacific Northwest.
Rocky Reach Dam's visitor center features a seasonal fish-viewing exhibit nicknamed 'Look a Salmon in the Eye.'
A juvenile fish bypass system, completed at Rocky Reach Dam in 2003, helps young salmon and steelhead migrate safely downstream.
Washington voters approved a statewide public utility district initiative in 1930, paving the way for Chelan County's own PUD.
Chelan County voters approved forming a Public Utility District in 1937, the same year Congress created the Bonneville Power Administration.
It took Chelan County PUD 11 years, until 1948, to complete its acquisition of Puget Sound Power & Light's local facilities.
Chelan County PUD acquired Washington Water Power Company's local hydroelectric assets in 1955.
Great Northern Railway crews built the original 2.63-mile Cascade Tunnel through Stevens Pass between 1897 and 1900.
Before the original Cascade Tunnel opened, Great Northern trains crossed Stevens Pass on eight dizzying switchbacks built in 1892.
An avalanche struck two stalled Great Northern trains at Wellington near Stevens Pass just after midnight on March 1, 1910, killing 96 people.
The Wellington avalanche disaster remains the deadliest avalanche in United States history.
Rescuers found the wreckage of the Wellington avalanche buried under roughly 40 feet of snow, about 150 feet below the tracks.
A second deadly avalanche near Corea, seven miles from Wellington, killed eight people on January 22, 1916.
By 1913, Great Northern Railway had built nine miles of protective snow-sheds over the tracks near Stevens Pass following the Wellington disaster.
Construction of the new Cascade Tunnel began on December 28, 1925, after President Lewis Hill authorized the project that Thanksgiving.
Crews broke through the new Cascade Tunnel from both ends on October 20, 1928.
A rock slide during construction of the new Cascade Tunnel killed four workers on November 8, 1928.
The new Cascade Tunnel, stretching 7.8 miles through solid granite, was dedicated on January 12, 1929, with President-elect Herbert Hoover speaking by radio.
Building the new Cascade Tunnel cost about $14 million to excavate, plus another $11.6 million to electrify, and took 1,750 workers 35 months.
The Cascade Tunnel's Stevens Pass rail corridor was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1976 as the Stevens Pass Historic District.
thoughts.source: Wikipedia: National Register of Historic Places listings in Chelan County, Washington

thoughts.text: The first apple seeds grown in the Pacific Northwest were planted at Fort Vancouver in the 1820s, decades before Chelan County's own orchards.
The Wenatchee Valley's first genuinely commercial apple orchard, the Patterson orchard, was planted in 1884.
By 1909, Wenatchee Valley growers were shipping about 2,000 freight cars of apples annually.
In the 1920s, Washington State surpassed New York to become the nation's leading apple-producing state.
The Wenatchee-Columbia Fruit Company licensed the Buster Brown comic character for apple advertising in 1912.
The Skookum brand launched a health-focused apple advertising campaign in 1914 to boost consumer demand.
During the Great Depression, apple prices collapsed so badly that the Wenatchee Valley was officially declared an 'economically stricken area' in 1935.
The Washington State Apple Advertising Commission was created by the state legislature in 1937 to promote the industry.
Wooden apple boxes, a Wenatchee Valley staple for decades, were largely replaced by cardboard packaging starting in 1958.
In 2019, the Gala apple surpassed the Red Delicious as Washington's leading commercial apple variety.
The Cosmic Crisp apple, developed by Washington State University, reached the market for the first time in 2019.
Chelan County farmers shipped 225 carloads of fruit in 1902, an 85 percent jump from the prior year, signaling the coming apple boom.
North central Washington's gold rush centered on the Blewett Mining District, where the first claims were filed in 1874.
A stone crushing arrastra built into bedrock at Blewett in 1863 is one of the oldest surviving ore-processing structures in Washington Territory.
By 1896, Blewett's mining district was running a 20-stamp ore-crushing mill at the mouth of Culver Gulch.
Blewett was named for Seattle mining investor Edward Blewett, whose company controlled many of the district's claims.
Blewett's stamp mill shut down in 1905 when the main gold vein ran out, though some mining continued there until 1911.
The Blewett Arrastra was added to the National Register of Historic Places on September 17, 1974.
The Manson area's town site was surveyed and graded in 1911, taking its name from Manson Backus, father of a local land company president.
Orchardists Peter Wapato and Ben Martin had already planted apple orchards near Manson before 1890, decades ahead of the town's founding.
The Chelan Box and Manufacturing Company was a major Manson employer from 1931 until its 1967 closure.
A fire destroyed Manson's associated sawmill in 1969, ending decades of local timber processing.
Squilchuck State Park, established in 1952, sits below Mission Ridge about 8 miles south of Wenatchee.
Lake Chelan State Park was created in 1942 and opened to the public in 1943, covering 139 acres on the lake's southwest shore.
Daroga State Park takes its name from the Auvil brothers, David, Robert, and Grady, whose orchard land it once was.
Daroga State Park's land was partly flooded when Rocky Reach Dam's reservoir, Lake Entiat, formed behind the new dam.
Washington State Parks began operating Daroga State Park in 1990 under a lease with Chelan County PUD, which still owns the land.
Lincoln Rock State Park, established in 1980, is named for a Columbia River cliff formation resembling Abraham Lincoln's profile.
Nearby Turtle Rock Island became a separated 150-acre nature preserve when Lake Entiat formed behind Rocky Reach Dam in the 1960s.
The U.S. Forest Service created the Chelan National Forest on July 1, 1908, covering nearly 2.5 million acres.
The Chelan National Forest merged with the Okanogan National Forest in 1921 and was renamed Okanogan National Forest in 1955.
Wildfires that began August 23, 1970, in Chelan County's Wenatchee National Forest burned 122,000 acres over 15 days.
The 1970 Wenatchee National Forest fires began as more than 200 lightning-sparked blazes that merged into five major fires.
Fighting the 1970 Chelan County forest fires required 8,500 firefighters and cost roughly $13 million to suppress.
Researchers studying the 1970 Chelan County burn area found evidence of earlier major fires dating to around 1830 and 1790.
The 2015 Sleepy Hollow Fire burned through Wenatchee's east side, destroying dozens of homes and businesses within city limits.
Planning for what became the North Cascades Highway began in the 1890s, before Washington's earliest legislature funded a cross-mountain wagon road in 1893.
An 1896 attempt to build the Cascade Wagon Road toward Stehekin stalled by 1899 due to flooding and steep terrain, leaving only a pack trail.
Local promoters formed the North Cross-State Highway Association in 1953 to push for a modern road across the North Cascades.
On September 29, 1968, nearly 1,000 people attended a ceremony dedicating a rough dirt version of the North Cascades Highway at Rainy Pass.
Governor Dan Evans and U.S. Senator Warren Magnuson both attended the 1968 North Cascades Highway dedication, with Magnuson arriving by helicopter.
The completed North Cascades Highway officially opened on September 2, 1972, after nearly 80 years of planning and construction.
Building the final stretch of the North Cascades Highway between 1959 and 1972 cost about $23.9 million.
The Port of Chelan County was created after voters approved it by an 8,086-to-3,520 margin in a November 1958 election.
The Port of Chelan County was originally chartered to promote Columbia River barge traffic before pivoting toward industrial development.
By 1959, the Port of Chelan County had begun acquiring former orchard land that became the Olds Station Business Park.
Wenatchee's downtown historic core was listed as the Downtown Wenatchee Historic District on the National Register in 2008.

thoughts.text: HistoryLink.org, a key source for Washington history, launched its prototype on May 1, 1998, and formally debuted on January 15, 1999.
HistoryLink.org bills itself as the nation's first online encyclopedia of state and local history created specifically for the internet.
In 1863, the area that would become Chelan County was organized as part of a short-lived jurisdiction called Ferguson County, later renamed Yakima County.
Before Chelan County existed, its territory was reassigned among Stevens, Yakima, and Kittitas counties as Washington Territory's boundaries were repeatedly redrawn.
Washington achieved statehood on November 11, 1889, a decade before Chelan County itself was created.
A trading post was established near modern Rock Island as early as 1867, decades before the town or dam existed.
Grant County was carved out of Douglas County in 1909, reshaping the region's county map a decade after Chelan County's own creation.
By the 2020 census, Chelan County's population had grown to 79,074 residents, more than 20 times its 1900 count.
Chelan County's Hispanic and Latino population share rose from about 19 percent in 2000 to nearly 28 percent by 2020.
Wenatchee's population exploded nearly eightfold in a decade, from 452 in 1900 to about 4,050 by 1910, after the railroad's arrival.
Congressman Tom Foley and Miss Washington Highways Jeannine Marie Gill both took part in the 1968 North Cascades Highway dedication ceremony.
Rocky Reach Dam has upgraded its turbines since 1995 with fish-friendly Kaplan designs meant to reduce harm to migrating salmon.
Rock Island Dam's original 1928 federal license application named it as the first hydroelectric project ever proposed to span the Columbia River.
Cashmere's early one-room schoolhouse, built in Brender Canyon, opened its doors in 1889.
Cashmere's Minerva Club, a women's civic organization, began meeting in 1905 and formally organized on January 17, 1906.
Frederick Schmitten opened a wooden fruit-box factory in Cashmere's Brender Canyon in 1902, supplying the growing apple trade.
The Chelan County Fair was established in Cashmere in 1953.
Cashmere's beloved 'Tiny's' fruit stand opened in 1953, burned in 1972, reopened in 1974, and finally closed in 1981.
East Wenatchee's Eastmont High School opened its doors in 1955.
East Wenatchee's Eastmont Shopping Center was redeveloped into the Wenatchee Valley Mall in 1978.
An explosion during construction killed Major John T. Fancher in April 1928; the East Wenatchee airfield was later named Fancher Field in his memory.
Douglas County commissioners attempted to force a disincorporation vote on East Wenatchee in 1987, though the city remained incorporated.
The first sizable irrigation ditch in the Wenatchee area, the Lockwood Ditch, was already being used by settlers as early as 1872.
Wenatchee received its first electric lights in 1903, powered by L. V. Wells's small generator on the Squilchuck River.
Wenatchee's Commercial Club, formed in 1903 under president John Arthur Gellatly, spearheaded early efforts to market the valley's apples nationally.
Wenatchee installed a rudimentary sewer system and began oiling and electrifying its streets in 1909.
The Wenatchee Golf and Country Club was established in 1924.
An airfield northeast of East Wenatchee, established in 1926, later became the site of Pangborn Memorial Airport.
Entiat's Quaker Church was established in 1906, the same year the Entiat Telephone and Telegraph Company was incorporated.
Entiat's first newspaper, the Entiat Times, began publishing in 1913 under editor Edward P. Murphy.
A Columbia River sternwheeler called the Pringle sank near Entiat in 1907.
Major Hiram Chittenden began clearing hazardous rapids on the Entiat River in 1907 to improve river navigation.
The Entiat Townsite Company's ownership of the town's land was upheld by the Washington State Supreme Court on November 22, 1917.
By 2020, Entiat's population had grown to 1,290, more than triple its 1960 population of 357.
Rufus Woods purchased the Wenatchee Daily World newspaper in 1907, going on to champion the Grand Coulee Dam idea for decades.
The Wenatchee area's Chinese mining camps in the 1860s left behind gold-processing sites still studied by historians today.
Chelan's Chelan Water Power Company, an early hydroelectric venture, was purchased by Morrison McMillan Kingman in early 1899.
The Chelan Electric Company bought out the town's earlier water power company in 1906, consolidating local hydroelectric control.
Washington Water Power Company acquired Chelan's hydroelectric interests in 1925 and received a 50-year federal power license in early 1926.
A promotional 'Board of Trade' brochure touting the new town of Chelan was distributed to prospective settlers in 1891.
Chelan's first Catholic parish was organized in 1904, the same year the Chelan Leader newspaper reported record numbers of tourists visiting the lake.
A planned electric railway around Lake Chelan, proposed by the Chelan Railroad & Navigation Company in 1903, was never actually built.
The Wapato Irrigation Company delivered its first water to Chelan-area farmland in 1911.
Rail service was extended to a new Chelan Station on the lake's north shore in 1914.
Chelan's population reached 896 by 1920 and grew to 1,403 residents by 1930.
By 2010, the city of Chelan's population had grown to 3,890, nearly double its count in 1980.
In 2012, Chelan's Historic Downtown Association and the city itself were jointly recognized as an 'Outstanding Partnership.'
